💡 Key Takeaways
  • Petit Planet marks Hoyoverse’s maiden voyage into the life sim genre popularized by games like Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, and, most recently, Pokémon Pokopia.
  • Recent findings suggest that the game’s premise centers on a customizable protagonist who sets out to populate their own personal planet (which is about the size of King Kai’s world from Dragon Ball Z).
  • Recent findings suggest that story is rarely a hook for a genre that largely promotes creating your own fun through the emergent moments with your neighbors and friends in multiplayer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Petit Planet marks Hoyoverse’s maiden voyage into the life sim genre popularized by games like Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, and, most recently, Pokémon Pokopia. The creators of Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero have crafted well-received, lucrative free-to-play gacha games across several disparate genres; Petit Planet, fittingly, sees it try to attract yet another world of players. It’s been a year since I first played Petit Planet’s initial alpha test, and I spent a couple of more hours exploring its cozy cosmos at the Hoyoverse Media Tour in Seoul, South Korea. Although what I played has not dramatically changed my opinion of the game – it remains a delightful, if familiar, good time – speaking to its lead designer who goes by the single name Murphy and lead artist Yunli Huang helped shed light on how Petit Planet will differentiate itself from contemporaries and its approach to multiplayer, storytelling, and monetization.

Recent findings suggest that the game’s premise centers on a customizable protagonist who sets out to populate their own personal planet (which is about the size of King Kai’s world from Dragon Ball Z). Although you are ostensibly human, everyone else is a talking animal. Your mentor of sorts is a chillax sheepdog named Mobai, who enjoys wearing straw hats and dropping his catchphrase/life mantra “Mo worries” and “Mo Rush.” The business-minded Glenn the Squirrel is a shopkeeper and seems like a cuter, less aggressive Tom Nook. Yunghou is a shy fox who enjoys farming and has the slightest hint of a southern accent. These critters and many more inhabit your planet, which you’ll grow from an empty (but vibrant) rock into a bustling village filled with homes, businesses, crops, decor, and, of course, neighbors.

Recent findings suggest that story is rarely a hook for a genre that largely promotes creating your own fun through the emergent moments with your neighbors and friends in multiplayer. Still, after Pokémon Pokopia presented an unexpectedly wild and fascinating tale, I ask if players should bother getting invested in a grander narrative à la Genshin Impact. The short answer seems to be “not so much.”.

Industry observers note that “Unlike other Hoyoverse games, there is no such main plot,” Murphy explains in my group interview. “There will be a main story at the beginning, but the main purpose is just to guide the players, get more familiar with the setting and the world. But the whole narrative of this game will be more fragmented. For example, if you look at those descriptions of those items, there will be a lot of content and narrative behind it. If you look at the description of creatures, many of them are real creatures in real world, and you get to learn more knowledge of this creature by reading those descriptions. And also, we've developed a very comprehensive narrative for each of our neighbors, so that is also part of our, called like, main plot, main narrative, because we want to make this world more like more lively and a more livable world. So that is how we treat narrative in this game.".

According to recent reports, while players who enjoy a substantial story to propel them through a game may be disappointed, those looking to unwind with a laid-back experience should be pleased. Hoyoverse is designing Petit Planet to be a no-pressure experience to enjoy at your leisure, hence why it emphasizes it as a life sim more than a management sim. There are no complicated stats to manage; simple inputs make it easy to pick up and play; imperfection is encouraged, with Hoyoverse comparing the experience to doodling as a child: your creation may not be perfect, but you had fun bringing your imagination to life.

I spent the first hour of my roughly two-and-a-half-hour session starting from scratch to see if any notable changes were made to this introductory portion in the last year. If there are any differences, they’re imperceptible because I wen went through the same onboarding of learning how to catch bugs and fish, building your first home, inviting your first neighbor, and farming crops, all while growing a magical sapling that, after performing enough tasks, blooms into a full tree that brings new life and mechanics to your world as it grows. Performing special tasks for residents, from completing requests to simply interacting with them, grows their bond, which, when high enough, will entice them to move in. For veteran genre fans, it’s a familiar song and dance. What I did notice this time around is how refreshingly quick the onboarding is. You have all of these foundational mechanics within the first 45 to 50 minutes, which is a nice pace. It was a good refresher for some foundational mechanics I’d forgotten since I last played, but it created an appetite to dive deeper.

According to recent reports, thankfully, Hoyoverse provided a second build set many hours into the game to give an idea of how planets can evolve. This build was set during winter, one of Petit Planet’s revolving seasons that alter the environment and introduce themed cosmetics and decor for players and residents. Sporting winter gear, I ran around the snow-covered planet, which was densely populated with shops, homes, and neighbors. I was initially greeted by unfamiliar faces named Trixie and Kookoo, who provided weather forecasts and news reports reminiscent of Isabelle from Animal Crossing and Callie and Marie from Splatoon. My sparse quest log was tricky to tackle since they revolved around mechanics I had no context for, such as setting up Vignettes. These are essentially templates for unique scenes filled out by dropping the correct furniture pieces in their layout; in this case, I had to set up an outdoor movie on the beach.

Recent findings suggest that I only spent roughly an hour with this late build, and my biggest takeaway was simply how dense and lovely the village looked. A lot of work went into crafting this build, which boasted a farm filled with different crops (with unlockable recipes to create dishes from them), crafting tables to build furniture from collectible blueprints, and several shops, including Glenn’s to purchase a revolving selection of decor items. None of what I saw surprised me, however. Petit Planet so far checks many of the boxes you’d expect and want from a life sim. My cursory tour of a later-game planet did little to reveal any big latest ideas, but what I did experience seemed perfectly cromulent.

Sources indicate that my biggest question regards multiplayer. As much as I enjoy Animal Crossing: Latest Horizons and Pokémon Pokopia as solo experiences, playing with friends feels like a mean joke because of the tedious number of hoops to jump through just to invite other players into your world. And even once your buddy arrives, interactions are disappointingly limited. When I ask if Petit Planet offers a comparatively frictionless multiplayer experience, Murphy vaguely assures smoother sailing. “The multiplayer experience is a very important part of our game because, just as the interaction with NPCs, the interaction with other players is also a form of building up emotional connection to this game, and we want to provide that kind of experience to our players.” More specifically, Murphy cites features such as dynamic server load adjustments based on player counts and the option to allow or ban visiting players from taking resources from your planet to prevent griefing.

As a free-to-play Hoyoverse game, monetization is a major talking point. In Petit Planet’s case, the team agrees that rolling for neighbors gacha-style would be strange and defeats the spirit of the genre. Instead, all monetization will revolve around cosmetics; players can unlock latest furniture and themed decor sets, outfits, and other cosmetic accessories for their character. Unlocking a full themed set of decor earns currency points, and there are myriad reward meters to fill for performing mundane tasks like greeting residents or catching bugs. It remains to be seen if and how Petit Planet’s progression begins nudging players into opening their wallets, but Hoyoverse promises it will be an experience that deemphasizes grinding.

I also briefly checked out the recently revealed Switch 2 version of Petit Planet. My impressions after about 15 minutes of playtime: it’s fine. It sometimes ran noticeably hitchier than the PC version I spent most of my time with, but it seems perfectly adequate so far and, hopefully, will be a smooth experience when it rolls out sometime next year.

Since life sims require more than a couple of hours to fully reveal their quality, it was tough to get a read on Petit Planet even with this fresh showing. The game looks beautiful thanks to Hoyoverse’s signature sharp and colorful visual style. It has a relaxing vibe, and feels mechanically decent for the most part. In short, it seems broadly fine and like a respectable take on the genre. I suspect its biggest appeal will be that it will receive what Animal Crossing: New Horizons lacked: years of constant, substantial support.

Hoyoverse is very good about keeping fans of its games well fed with regular updates for years on end, and I don’t expect it to stop now. The idea of a seemingly well-made spin on Animal Crossing that’s free to download and, unless it completely bombs, will almost certainly receive years of fresh content is enticing on paper. I imagine this is the reason Petit Planet is coming to Switch 2 next year, where it can lure in Animal Crossing and Pokopia players before other consoles. PC and mobile players, meanwhile, must only wait until December 4 when Petit Planet fully launches to see if it has the chops to stand alongside the coziest giants of the genre.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past two decades, if you were looking for an upscale three-row German SUV, the Audi Q7 or its performance-oriented SQ7 sibling was likely on your shopping list. Both have long delivered on style, family-friendliness, and luxury.

The mid-size Audi SUVs are completely upcoming for 2027, but the automaker has been careful not to stray too far from a blueprint that has proved so successful. With this latest generation, the Q7’s design has been brought up to speed with the rest of the Audi lineup. That means softer edges, a more muscular stance, and a lot more digital displays inside.

Industry observers note that while the Q7’s dimensions grow slightly in most directions, it’s still roughly the same size as before, and its three-row layout could best be described as a 5+2, as the cramped rearmost chairs are best used by children and only in a pinch. If you need more space, there’s now a full-size Q9 model that’s larger inside and out.

See all results for upcoming 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near 98115.

The Q7 does gain a sought-after second-row feature: optional captain’s chairs. Choosing the two-seat second row reduces seat count from seven to six, but it also decreases the risk of sibling quarrels.

Industry observers note that speaking of the cabin, we’ve complained that Audi’s latest interiors haven’t lived up to the standard set by the firm’s earlier efforts, but the new Q7 represents a reversal of that trend. Granted, the models we sampled were well-optioned examples, but the interior materials are premium, and even the $72,295 base model gets genuine leather upholstery and real wood inlays.

Sources indicate that upgrade to a higher Q7 trim, and you’ll enjoy luxuries such as soft-close doors, a Bang & Olufsen stereo, and massaging front seats. The SQ7 comes in just one trim level, starting at $100,095, and it’s comprehensively equipped with only a few available packages, most of them designed to improve performance and handling.

Special attention has been paid to the SUV’s exterior lighting elements. There are a lot of them, and some are genuinely useful, none more so than Audi’s digital matrix headlights.

Not only do these high-tech headlamps deliver a shockingly bright view of the road ahead, but they also sense oncoming vehicles and will temporarily deactivate some of their bulbs to avoid blinding other motorists. A set of OLED taillights illuminate in different ways depending on context, with the intent to help communicate with other drivers: For example, if another vehicle is too close to the Q7’s rear bumper in traffic, the lights will illuminate with additional brightness as a warning to back off.

Other flashy features push into gimmick territory. There’s a light-up grille, a customizable taillamp and daytime-running-light signature, and a system that projects arrows on the street surface to indicate which direction the driver is signaling. Are blinkers no longer enough? Luckily, if you don’t want your Audi lighting up like a Christmas tree, some of these features can be deactivated via the Q7’s infotainment system.

See all results for new 2027 Audi Q7 for sale near 98115.

Industry observers note that speaking of infotainment, there are a lot of screens inside the Q7. A large infotainment touchscreen is expected, surely, but there’s also a digital gauge display, a passenger’s display, and an optional head-up display.

While the previous-generation Q7 offered a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four as standard with a turbocharged 3.0-liter V-6 as an upgrade, the 2027 model ditches the four-banger altogether, making a V-6 standard. This version’s six—a turbo 2.9-liter—packs 429 horsepower, a 94-hp advantage over the outgoing model.

A twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8 has always powered the SQ7, and the newly introduced generation is no different. It also gets more power, jumping from 500 horsepower in 2026 to 591 horsepower in 2027.

It has been revealed that acceleration is plentiful in the Q7, which makes quick work of highway passing maneuvers and will beat most regular traffic off the line with a quick stab of the throttle. Audi estimates a 4.8-second 60-mph time.

Industry observers note that the SQ7 is another animal altogether. While both SUVs have launch control, using it in the SQ7 results in a giggle-inducing run to highway speeds. Audi wagers a 60-mph run would take just 3.7 seconds. The V-8’s muted burble is a bonus.

Industry observers note that confident and predictable handling, an Audi touchstone, remains the default. While all Q7s come with Balanced, Dynamic, and Comfort drive modes, those with the optional air-spring suspension benefit most, with each mode delivering noticeably different ride qualities. SQ7s get air springs as standard but can be optioned with a sport-tuned version of the system, which lowers the ride height 1.2 inches in Dynamic mode and firms everything up to the max.

Recent findings suggest that SQ7 models also feature a retuned all-wheel-drive system with more rear bias. Unlike previous Audi performance SUVs, which were short on driving drama, the latest SQ7’s more fun-loving nature shines on twisty roads with that newfound rear-end boogie. Our test drive took us down some of northern California’s twistiest roads, and both SUVs proved entertaining and luxurious.

Industry observers note that with this upcoming generation, Audi has boosted the Q7 and SQ7’s swank factor. It has modernized their styling without introducing a new polarizing design language while adding options buyers want. Retaining the Q7’s just-right size and keeping the focus on refined, performance-oriented road manners is the hedge that will keep it near the top of the shopping list of enthusiast drivers who need family-sized space.

10 Best Games That Showcase The Xbox Brand

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft’s gaming brand, Xbox, has finally reached the momentous milestone of existing for 25 years, with all four generations of Xbox console greeting gaming memories that will last lifetimes for those who played them throughout the 21st century.
  • These days, however, in the wake of poor direction during the Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S eras, Xbox is struggling to retain a healthy gamer population, with many gamers choosing instead to play games on Nintendo or PlayStation due those platforms’ vast variety of exclusive titles.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft’s gaming brand, Xbox, has finally reached the momentous milestone of existing for 25 years, with all four generations of Xbox console greeting gaming memories that will last lifetimes for those who played them throughout the 21st century.

These days, however, in the wake of poor direction during the Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S eras, Xbox is struggling to retain a healthy gamer population, with many gamers choosing instead to play games on Nintendo or PlayStation due those platforms’ vast variety of exclusive titles.

With Xbox having recently reached its 25th anniversary and the next generation of Xbox consoles, Project Helix, expected to debut in a few years, here’s a look back at 10 exclusive games that best showcase the Xbox brand and may potentially entice people to try an Xbox console.

Many fans of the British game developer, Rare, likely recognize them for creating Nintendo-centric titles like Banjo-Kazooie or Donkey Kong Country but under Microsoft’s ownership, one of the best games they ever released was Viva Piñata.

A life simulation game, Viva Piñata is set on the wondrous Piñata Island and has players restore a garden there with the goal of attracting, raising, and defending the local population of living piñata animals so that they can be eventually shipped off across the globe to become the center of attention at parties.

Viva Piñata encapsulates how creative, fun, and unique Xbox games can be and, while there hasn’t been a new Viva Piñata game in over 18 years, people today can still easily play it and other classic Rare games via the compilation Rare Replay.

One of the best games that showcases the absolute power and capabilities of modern Xbox consoles is Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024, the latest entry in the long-running Microsoft Flight Simulator series.

Like many flight simulator games, Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 allows players to learn how to fly planes in both first and third-person but this game is the most advanced flight simulator yet as players can learn how to fly other real and fictional aircraft in numerous locations across the globe.

For example, people can fly Halo’s Pelican dropship over Yosemite National Park, the Goodyear Blimp over London, a DG Flugzeugbau DG-1000 over Mount Fuji, a Airbus Helicopters H225 over the Stilt Villages of Papua Fresh Guinea and more.

Viva Piñata was very memorable but it wasn’t the most popular video game Rare made under Microsoft’s ownership, with that title instead going to the hit cartoonish pirate multiplayer game Sea of Thieves.

Played primarily in first-person, Sea of Thieves allows players to create and customize their very own pirate and ship as they set sail alone or with a crew of friends into monster-infested waters in search of treasure and glory across the sea.

Sea of Thieves might have had rough start when it first launched in 2018 but in the years since, it has truly shined to become the definitive pirate multiplayer experience thanks to its comedic gameplay and eventful updates adding newly introduced areas to explore and supernatural sea creatures to fight.

For a while, Xbox was the best platform to play western RPGs on and, during the original Xbox era, one of the best exclusive games to showcase this status was Bioware’s legendary Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic.

A third-person round-based RPG, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic is set roughly 4,000 years before the events of the Star Wars films and follows an amnesiac warrior as they set out to stop the Jedi turned Sith Darth Malak from conquering the galaxy with the mysterious Star Forge.

While KOTOR’s gameplay hasn’t aged perfectly in the 23 years since its launch, its story, characters, and world designs have remained immaculate, with its characters going on to influence many other Star Wars stories and it still featuring one of the greatest gaming twists surrounding the character of Darth Revan.

Since the days of the Xbox 360, Microsoft has often invested and supported small game developers with immense potential, leading to the release of games like Braid, Ori and the Blind Forest, and the subject for this entry, Cuphead.

Studio MDHR’s debut title, Cuphead is a 2D run and gun game with visuals inspired by rubberhose-style cartoons of the 1920s and 30s, similar to Steamboat Willie, following the brothers Cuphead and Mugman as they set out to collect soul contracts from various bosses in order to save their souls from the Devil.

While Cuphead was only a timed exclusive on the Xbox One, it represents the brand’s ability to support small game development studios and uplift experimental titles into gaming stardom as Cuphead has gone on to sell millions of copies and become a highly successful multimedia franchise.

Racing has always been at the core of Xbox gaming from the early days of Project Gotham Racing to the more modern Forza Motorsport titles and while none of these games have been as popular as Mario Kart, one has managed to become the most advanced, realistic racing game yet: Forza Horizon 6.

The latest entry in the ongoing Forza Horizon series, Forza Horizon 6 has players take to the urban and rural streets of Tokyo, Japan in over 500 cars as they strive to qualify for the Horizon Festival or simply explore the many beautiful landscapes of Japan alone or with friends.

In a similar way to how Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 became the premier modern flight simulator, Forza Horizon 6 has become the premier realistic racing game thanks to its hyperrealistic visuals, vast automotive and track customization options, and dynamic environments.

KOTOR is one of the best RPGs to ever debut on an Xbox console but it’s not the brand’s premier exclusive RPG, with that honor instead going to 2004’s Fable and the greater Fable franchise.

Originally pitched to be a fantasy RPG that would have allowed players to have kids in-game, and witness plant life grow among other promises, the original Fable wound up being a very charming, British humor fantasy RPG following a young boy as he set out to become the hero of Albion.

While the first Fable didn’t meet all of its creator, Peter Molyneux, aspirations, it sequels did slowly start to achieve all of Molyneux’s promises and more, becoming the source of many fond memories to the point that Forza Horizon 6’s own Playground Games is rebooting the series with 2027’s Fable.

One of the most recent games that best showcase the Xbox brand’s storytelling capability and multiplayer potential is The Coalition’s Gears of War: E-Day, the sixth mainline entry in the Gears of War series and prequel to the first Gears game.

Like its predecessors, Gears of War: E-Day is a third-person cover shooter with updated maneuverability but what made it really shine is its emotional story following COG soldiers Marcus Fenix, Dominic Santiago, Mags Carter, and Lucas Reyes as they face the first horrifying Locust invasion on Emergence Day.

Gears has always been known for its gory, action-packed gameplay as well as its heartfelt story following people face seemingly insurmountable nightmarish forces and E-Day proves that Gears can still deliver horrifying, emotional yet hopeful gaming narratives 20 years after its first debuted in 2006.

The Xbox 360 era was arguably Xbox at its best and most successful largely in part due to Microsoft investing in several permanent and timed exclusive titles alike, such when Microsoft and Mojang worked together to make the Xbox 360 the first console home for the global sensation that was Minecraft.

While Minecraft was already highly popular on PC, Minecraft: Xbox 360 Edition helped introduce millions of console players to the blocky survival game for the first time via Xbox Live Arcade in 2012 and led many to grow up with the game as it evolved and expanded with every update.

Minecraft: Xbox 360 Edition’s success ultimately led to Microsoft acquiring Mojang in 2014 and since then, the two companies have worked together to make Minecraft one of the most successful multimedia franchises of all time through the release of numerous Minecraft updates, spinoffs, and adaptations.

The Halo franchise is as integral to Xbox as Sonic the Hedgehog is to Sega and Super Mario is to Nintendo and while there have been many fantastic Halo titles released over the years, I would argue that the best entry in the series to showcase the Xbox brand is the FPS prequel, Halo: Reach.

Bungie’s last Halo title, Halo: Reach has players embody the customizable Spartan-III Noble Six as they join the Spartan-II and III squad of Noble Team in defending the human military world of Reach from an alien Covenant invasion a few months before the events of Halo: Combat Evolved.

While Reach’s campaign is a ton of fun on its own, I believe Reach is the best Halo title to represent the Xbox brand because it remains the most complete Halo title to date as it introduced with four-player campaign co-op, playable Elites, Firefight, Forge, Theater, Infection, Grifball, and more fun modes and features.

It has been revealed that that’s an incredibly healthy player base, but more than that, it’s more than double the previous record holder, Nioh 2, which peaked at 41,325 concurrent players in 2021. #143646. Industry News: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1330 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed.
  • For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works.
  • But the new findings raise an crucial question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.

For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.

But the new findings raise an crucial question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?

"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a upcoming study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity.".

A Fresh Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI.

The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.

If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.

"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," notes Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.

The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.

Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.

AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story.

The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.

AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.

According to recent reports, "The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," notes Kar.

It has been revealed that the findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.

Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.

That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.

"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," indicates Kar.

Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior.

It has been revealed that the implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.

If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.

Recent findings suggest that "Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.

Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.

The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.

Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain.

Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.

By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.

It has been revealed that "Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," claims Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline.".

A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.

To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.

Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a fresh approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.

The discovery could help guide the development of a upcoming generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.

8 Hard to Beat Game Boy JRPGs

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Back in the day we didn’t have a ton of ways to check how to beat something or find any guides that would be readily available.
  • Even for some of the best JRPGs available you could spend a ton of hours just getting through one part.
  • A lot of the games on this list are from series and part of that is because most games that released on the original Game Boy were not JRPGs as they weren’t quite as substantial in the states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in the day we didn’t have a ton of ways to check how to beat something or find any guides that would be readily available. A lot of the time you just sort of muddle through until you figure out exactly what you’re supposed to do.

Even for some of the best JRPGs available you could spend a ton of hours just getting through one part. It was a glorious time where conquering that challenge felt rewarding because of how difficult that particular JRPG section may have been.

A lot of the games on this list are from series and part of that is because most games that released on the original Game Boy were not JRPGs as they weren’t quite as substantial in the states. Regardless, any game on this list is sure to give you a rough go of it if you aren’t prepared.

It has been revealed that while Rolan’s Curse II is a bit more of an action-RPG, the game still takes several notes from JRPGs at the time and typically is counted amongst them. Instead of traditional turn-based mechanics, the game uses real-time combat making it more difficult than other JRPGs.

Recent findings suggest that many would go on to call it a Zelda-like game, but thanks to the inclusion of a party system with several characters it does fit the JRPG genre. The real-time aspect of the game made it more difficult to play, but also could force players into continuous encounters making things escalate in difficulty rather promptly.

The original Rolan’s Curse is a bit different from the second entry since it doesn’t include a cast of characters to play as. Much as you might imagine the game centered around the same core principals although the upgrades and such are for your character.

Two things specifically make this one a bit tougher, one being that there’s limited ways to recover yourself and second the combat is fairly punishing. It’s a game that definitely requires you to play with focus and without that focus you’ll find yourself dying a lot.

In a recent development, the very first game to ever be released in the SaGa series, The Final Fantasy Legend has some interesting history behind it. The game featured fantasy and sci-fi elements alongside each other as players built a party to take on the challenge ahead of them.

The difficulty of the game stemmed from how unusual the character development systems were combined with some harder combat as the game progressed. Players who didn’t take advantage of the systems for leveling would find themselves at an extreme disadvantage.

Sources indicate that despite the title of this one, it’s actually the first game in what would eventually become the Mana series. A much closer game to Zelda than many would imagine, but mostly thanks to weapons and such doubling as exploration tools.

Outside of that the game featured a party system in which an NPC could tag along on an adventure to help out. The real difficulty of this one comes from keeping tabs on your timing and positioning where even a small mistake could be costly.

In a recent development, A strange game for the time period that used a first-person view instead of top down for a fantasy JRPG. It took notes from things like Dragon Quest in terms of giving players the ability to investigate and engage with the world on a deeper level.

Since everything was fairly cryptic and there wasn’t much information given, players could often find themselves stuck on certain parts of the game. It took a lot more effort to get from one place to another if you didn’t want to do the investigating you had to.

This game changed some of the formula from the first one and introduced a tried and true JRPG mechanic, a party system. Rather than controlling one character the player now had a party to manage, but still used a first-person turn-based mechanic for gameplay.

Recent findings suggest that arguably a bit harder than the first game since now you dolled out resources amongst a party over just an individual. You could, of course, still miss plenty of things without investigating which led to players being at an extreme disadvantage some of the time.

Probably one of the crazier games in the series with a lot of going on in just about every part of the game. The odd fantasy and sci-fi bits of the game mixed gave players a lot of choice in how they handled leveling their character and gaining equipment.

Recent findings suggest that in true JRPG fashion, what makes the game unique also makes it incredibly difficult. By transforming your party members into various races based on items you gave them could really screw up your journey if you weren’t careful.

Sources indicate that many JRPGs of the time period were doing some experimental work with various mechanics to spice up how their games played. Final Fantasy Legend II was no exception to this rule and even took it a step farther making it arguably one of the hardest JRPGs for the time.

Even the best JRPGs have some form of resource management, but those usually don’t apply to the story. MAGI, a collectible resource in the game, could be used to both enhance your character or progress the story forcing a difficult choice between power and story.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Riot will take the Mid-Season Invitational to Spain in 2027, bringing a top-tier League of Legends event back to Europe for the first time since the Worlds 2024 final in London. Its one-off, expanded First Stand in China will also change Split 1 for the LEC, with the full details due in January.

According to recent reports, europe will host a top-tier League of Legends event again in 2027. Riot set out its international calendar on 13 November, the eve of the Worlds 2026 final. The Mid-Season Invitational goes to Valencia. London’s staging of the Worlds 2024 final was the last time the continent held an international League of Legends tournament.

For British fans, that puts a top-tier event within Europe next year. Riot has not yet given dates or ticket details for the Feria de Valencia event.

Spain’s last international League of Legends event came in 2019. That year, Madrid’s Palacio Vistalegre staged the Worlds quarter-finals and semi-finals. Valencia has never hosted one before.

Industry observers note that china will stage First Stand: All In at the start of the 2027 season. Riot calls this single edition its largest tournament ever.

According to recent reports, first Stand 2027 had originally been given to Southeast Asia. The bigger format took it to China instead. Southeast Asia will now host the event in 2028.

According to recent reports, the change reaches every regional league, including the LEC. The larger event will change Split 1, just as Fnatic, G2 and the other LEC teams rebuild their rosters. In 2026, First Stand ran from 16 to 22 March, between the two regional splits. A bigger event at the start of the year leaves less certainty about how that window will look in 2027.

Riot has not yet said how many teams will take part or how they will qualify. Until then, LEC teams are building squads without knowing how many European places are on offer.

Industry observers note that worlds 2027 will be shared between two countries. The Swiss Stage goes to Nagoya, Japan. The quarter-finals and semi-finals move to the Suwon Convention Center in South Korea. The title decider goes to Seoul Arena, which is still under construction.

The arena was 81% built on 23 October. Work is due to finish in May 2027, with the venue opening in June 2027.

Industry observers note that the city is backing the event with public money. Seoul has set aside 1.369 billion won (about US$1.02 million) in its proposed 2027 budget to host the Worlds final and Fan Fest, Sheep Esports reported.

The 2026 calendar offers a reference point for the circuit’s rhythm. MSI ran from 28 June to 12 July, and Worlds from 15 October to 14 November. Riot has not confirmed whether the 2027 events will follow similar windows.

For LEC teams, clarity on the season opener in China is due in January.

Blizzard has recently been celebrating its major running games by hosting substantial livestreams to reveal some major changes, and it’s now Diablo’s turn. The Diablo series is 30 years-old, so this all just ties in nicely with some of the reveals planned for tonight’s showcase.

The Diablo 30th Anniversary Spotlight is set to kick off today at 2pm PT, 5pm ET, 10pm GMT.

Sources indicate that the biggest reason why you might want to tune in is, of course, that a whole chunk of the event will focus on Diablo 4. Blizzard will unveil the second class coming to the game with the Lord of Hatred expansion. The developer, of course, released the first of two classes - Paladin - immediately at the upcoming expansion’s initial reveal back in December.

Lord of Hatred is set to arrive April 28, and there’s even more it’s bringing to the core game that will be shown off during the livestream. Blizzard remarked we can expect a deeper look at the revamped skill trees, as well as endgame mechanics and features Lord of Hatred is set to introduce.

According to recent reports, beyond Diablo 4 itself, the showcase will feature updates on Diablo Immortal, and even Diablo 2: Resurrected. Blizzard hasn’t been teasing any other announcements, but many still hold out hope for a proper Diablo 1 remaster.

According to recent reports, as always, you’ll be able to watch the show live on Diablo 4’s official YouTube, and Twitch channels. We’ve embedded the Twitch player below for your convenience.
